title: Named executor of a will: first decisions (US)
dek: Understand nomination, court authority and estate duties before moving money, and check the local process if you cannot accept the executor role.
metaDescription: Understand nomination, court authority and estate duties before moving money, and check the local process if you cannot accept the executor role.

paragraphs: Being named executor in a US will nominates you for estate administration; it does not automatically prove you have authority to transact. First decide whether you can serve, locate the will, identify the applicable probate or alternative process, and protect urgent interests without distributing property. If appointed, you manage estate duties rather than simply hand out inheritances.

Your name may appear in a document written years ago, before the family circumstances or your own capacity changed. You can ask what the job involves before promising to do it. This is a first-decision guide, not a state-specific probate manual, tax opinion or instruction to take actions beyond your authority.

body.heading: Before accepting transactions as routine
items: Locate the original will and any amendments. Identify co-nominees and alternates without deciding contested validity yourself.
Ask the relevant court about will-deposit duties, the appointment process, any small-estate alternative, required notices and urgent deadlines.

If unsure about serving, ask about declining before undertaking substantive administration. Explain exactly what you have already done rather than assuming one call either commits you or means nothing.
List immediate care, security, insurance or business-continuity concerns and ask who may lawfully handle them pending appointment.
Gather an initial map of assets, debts and ownership. Separate possible estate assets from joint, beneficiary-designated or trust assets needing another route.
Keep a dated decision and expense record from the start. Do not mix estate receipts with your own spending or make informal promises of distributions.

body.heading: Authority comes before ordinary estate transactions
paragraphs: In New York, [the court appoints the fiduciary](https://www.nycourts.gov/help/when-someone-dies/fiduciary-estate). The court document and permitted powers matter when dealing with institutions. Other states use their own processes and terminology. Ask which evidence each institution needs rather than presenting the will as a universal withdrawal authorization.

A power of attorney used during life is not a substitute for the post-death estate process. Do not impersonate the deceased person online, transfer a balance into your own account, or sign a sale because a family member says the will makes it yours anyway. Ask about necessary temporary authority if a genuine urgent transaction cannot wait.

body.heading: The work after the proper authority is established
columns: Decision that must not be skipped
rows: Inventory, ownership evidence and secure records.
Which assets belong in this administration?
Supported date-of-death values and specialist advice where needed.
Is the value documented rather than guessed?
A schedule of notices, returns, liabilities and reserves.
Which rules, priorities and deadlines actually apply?
Approved accounting, receipts and closure evidence.
Have claims, taxes, restrictions and required approvals been resolved?

body.heading: Invented example: a house, an account and an old pension
paragraphs: A nominated executor finds a house with a mortgage, one sole-name bank account and a retirement statement naming an administrator. They record these as leads. They do not assume the pension is part of the probate estate, or promise the house to one sibling before checking ownership and the will.

They ask the court about appointment, the bank about required documents and the plan administrator about the benefit-claim route. The first useful output is a verified map and next-action list, not a total inheritance figure. If a mortgage or insurer needs immediate contact, they gather instructions and document who has authority for the action requested.

body.heading: Separate the deceased person's tax from estate administration
paragraphs: The [IRS administrator guidance](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/responsibilities-of-an-estate-administrator) distinguishes obligations involving the deceased person and the estate. Ask a qualified tax adviser which federal and state filings are required, who signs them and when. Do not assume that a small estate means no final income-tax work, or confuse estate income tax with estate transfer tax.

Where an estate identification number is needed, use the [official IRS EIN route](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/get-an-employer-identification-number), not an unsolicited paid intermediary. An EIN is not proof of court appointment. Ask the bank what authority and identification it requires before opening an estate account; do not create accounts merely to feel the process has started.

body.heading: Personal liability is about duties, not inheriting every debt
paragraphs: The [FTC explains that estate debts are generally paid from estate assets](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/debts-and-deceased-relatives), with exceptions affecting some personal obligations. An estate representative can also create problems by mishandling legal duties. Do not pay creditors in the order they call or distribute funds on the assumption that later claims can simply be ignored.

If liabilities may exceed assets, stop before paying or distributing and seek probate advice about priorities. The same applies to disputed wills, taxes you cannot assess, a business, foreign property, missing funds or a sale to yourself or another relative. A lawyer's fees, compensation and reimbursement arrangements should be agreed and checked against the will, law and any required approval; estate payment is not an unlimited guarantee.

items.line: I am nominated in the will and have not established transaction authority. Which steps preserve the estate, what appointment route applies, and what deadlines need attention now?
I do not think I can undertake administration. These are the actions I have already taken: [facts]. What is the correct local procedure for declining or, if already appointed, seeking release?

body.heading: Give the family process updates, not premature promises
paragraphs: Record receipts, values, provider responses and the basis for decisions. Agree a practical update channel so beneficiaries know what is confirmed and what remains unresolved. Being both a beneficiary and nominated executor does not remove the need to handle competing interests carefully.

Do not promise completion in a set number of weeks. Court processing, claims, tax questions, sales and disputes can each control the pace. Track actual milestones and ask for help with a specific blocked decision. Hiring help does not automatically transfer all your responsibilities; clarify who is doing what in writing.

items.q: Do I have to serve because the will names me?
items.a: Nomination does not mean you must silently take the job on. Ask the relevant court or probate attorney how to decline and explain anything you have already done. If you have been appointed, stepping down requires the proper release or replacement process; do not simply stop responding or hand the file to a relative.

items.q: Can I distribute money once I find the will?
items.a: Not simply because the will has been found. Authority, ownership, creditor procedures, tax obligations and any required approval must be checked. A distribution that seems obvious to the family can still be premature. Preserve the money and get advice before paying inheritances or moving estate funds into personal accounts.

items.q: Does the executor personally pay the estate's debts?
items.a: Not automatically from personal funds, but personal obligations and mistakes in administration can change the position. Ask about responsibility before making promises or payments. If the estate may be insolvent, get advice about claim priorities and required procedure instead of paying whichever creditor applies the most pressure.
